entries.title: Sixth beluga whale rescued from Canada dies in San Diego, following four deaths at the Shedd
entries.summary: <p>Another beluga whale rescued from the shuttered Marineland aquarium in Ontario, Canada, has died, SeaWorld in San Diego announced.</p><p>Cyprus, a 9-year-old beluga, stopped eating this weekend and declined quickly, said a Facebook post from the aquarium. He was initially doing well since arriving in San Diego in August, but belugas, like many species, can hide their discomfort or face underlying health concerns, the facility said.</p><p>That brings the total number of Marineland whales to die since being rescued to six, including four at Chicago's Shedd Aquarium and one at Oceanografic Valencia in Spain.</p><p>At the Shedd, the most recent death was Caspian, a 27-year-old female, that died Oct. 7. Peekachu, a 23-year-old female, died Aug. 25, and Rain, a 20-year-old female, died Sept. 2. Osiris, a 26-year-old female, died Sept. 21. The rescued beluga in Spain, Jelly Bean, died Sept. 18.</p><p>A resident beluga at the Shedd, Beethoven, also died recently at 34, likely due to age-related issues, the aquarium said.</p><p>Marineland closed this summer after facing financial ruin and loud criticism from animal rights activists, some of whom have also questioned the safety of transferring the whales to other aquariums.</p><p>The SeaWorld post said, "Like our colleagues at the other AZA-accredited facilities that rescued these belugas, we understood each animal would be navigating a significant transition and that their complete health picture, including conditions that may have developed over time, could only become clearer through ongoing assessment and care."</p><p>SeaWorld is still working to acclimate the rest of the belugas from Marineland, and staff acknowledged it would take time for the animals to adjust.</p><p>"The other rescued belugas in our care continue to be in stable health and remain under close monitoring as they continue to adjust to their surroundings," the aquarium said. "As we have indicated, this process will take a considerable amount of time. Our commitment to the health, well-being and care of these belugas, like every animal we rescue, continues." </p>

entries.title: Analyzing Game 1 of the WNBA Finals
entries.summary: <p>SAN FRANCISCO — You’re probably feeling pretty annoyed right now if you’re the Dream, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/wnba/2026/10/17/valkyries-fans-meet-coach-natalie-nakases-expectations-in-game-1-of-the-wnba-finals" >having lost a Game 1</a> in which you led for 75% of it, and had the Valkyries offense looking like a fish flopping on land.</p><p>In fact, the half-court offense appeared so halting and uncertain about where any openings were that I had to ask a couple of Bay Area journalists after the game what the Valkyries’ strategy on offense even is.</p><p>They said it was waiting for the Dream to make a mistake.</p><p>The problem with that is that the Dream don’t make very many. They’re long, quick, and in each other’s gaps. As a result, so many Valkyries possessions ended in a desperation heave, or a forced drive into Dream defenders that hadn’t been shifted.</p><p>The Dream enjoyed a lead for much of the third quarter until a Valkyries run — which included a Kiah Stokes tip-in, an unlikely roll on a Kaila Charles’ three-point shot, and a breakdown from the Dream leaving Charles wide open for a layup — gave them the lead.</p><p>Even through his normal stoicism, you could tell Dream coach Karl Smesko was very attuned to how luck and tiny mistakes swung the game in the Valkyries favor.</p><p>“I thought our team defended excellent, but when a game is this close even a couple breakdowns can make the difference,” Smesko said.</p><p>The problem that Smesko likely spent Sunday mulling over is that the Dream’s half-court offense was really no better than the Valkyries’. Though I’m no expert on the the Dream either, I can tell you that the one thing every half-court offense is supposed to do — swing the ball from one side of the court to the other — did not happen. Like the Valkyries, it was a lot of one pass then fire away.</p><p>“We had a couple of dry spells where we just weren’t working together as well as you need to against this [Valkyries] defense,” Smesko said.</p><p>They also turned their back on what had been working from the jump. Forward Angel Reese built them a lead in the first quarter, then only touched the ball in scoring position twice in the second half.</p><p>“Maybe that was just on me,” Reese said. “I wasn’t aggressive enough with the ball and trying to get the ball and to get to spots.<br>So definitely going to do a better job of that next game.”</p><p>Smesko also took responsibility, saying they need to do a better job getting the ball to Reese.</p><p>The bright side is that “giving Reese the ball” and actually moving the ball from side to side don’t really seem that difficult to correct heading into Game 2. The other bright side is that despite Dream superstar Rhyne Howard finishing with a measly 12 points, they still only lost by four. They also had two wide-open shots at the end that could have won the game.</p><p>“Naz [Hillmon] had a good look at three,” Smesko said. “Rhyne had a good look at three. We knock down either of those we’re not talking about whatever mistakes we made.</p><p>“But that’s what this game comes down to. You have two shots go in and out. At some point in the game, they bank in a three. We were right there. So that’s why it hurts a little bit. But it also motivates us. We know we’re capable of doing.”</p><p>This WNBA Finals represents a changing of the guard. The Valkyries and Dream knocked off the Aces and the Liberty, super-teams that have dominated the last five years, and they reached the pinnacle in large part by feasting on other teams’ mistakes.</p><p>Which is why Game 1 felt like such a staring contest; there just aren’t very many mistakes left to be mined.</p>

entries.title: Evanston, New Trier investigate reports of racist, homophobic slurs during football game at new Ryan Field
entries.summary: <p>Two suburban school districts are investigating after reports of homophobic and racist slurs at Friday night's football game between the two schools. Played at Northwestern University's newly opened Ryan Field, the game was supposed to be a season highlight for New Trier and Evanston Township high schools. More than 25,000 fans attended, according to some reports.</p><p>New Trier fans directed racist and homophobic comments toward members of the Evanston marching band, according to a joint statement from both districts' superintendents.</p><p>"Friday evening should have been an opportunity to celebrate our students, spirited competition, and the longstanding traditions of our two school communities," the statement said. "For the ETHS Marching Band, it was an especially meaningful opportunity to do what they love: share their talents and proudly represent their school. No student should leave an event where they came to perform, compete, or support their peers feeling that their dignity or belonging were demeaned."</p><p>Administrators at both districts are working together to investigate the reports and encourage anyone with information about the incident to contact their school's administration.</p>

entries.title: Bears beat Falcons 31-23 in QB Caleb Williams' return
entries.summary: <p>ATLANTA — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback Caleb Williams stepped up in the pocket, shuffled right and started sprinting toward the sideline. He looked downfield until he locked eyes with his biggest target, then threw across his body toward tight end Colston Loveland, who was sandwiched between two Falcons defenders at the goal line.</p><p>Loveland caught the ball as he was smacked by the two players for the first touchdown of the Bears’ 31-23 victory Sunday against the Falcons. Williams soon delivered another hit — a gentle head bump — before taking off his helmet and celebrating on the sideline.</p><p>‘‘Just let it rip,’’ Williams said. ‘‘Let the emotions rip.’’</p><p>It was a show of emotion a month in the making, ever since Williams suffered a torn right hamstring in the fourth quarter of a Week 2 loss against the Vikings. And it was a spark the Bears desperately needed in the wake of a 31-7 thrashing at the hands of the Packers a week ago.</p><p>Williams’ performance was much more than a ball of emotion, however. He was a stone-cold assassin, completing 30 of 36 passes for 305 yards and a 111.2 passer rating. He completed his first 12 passes, including a third-down hook-and-ladder to wide receiver Rome Odunze, who shoveled the ball to running back Roschon Johnson. It set up the touchdown to Loveland, who finished with a season-high 65 yards on six catches.</p><p>In a clean pocket, Williams went 24-for-24 for 248 yards, according to NFL Next Gen Stats. No NFL quarterback has completed that many passes without an incompletion since at least 2018.</p><p>‘‘Let the emotions fly,’’ Williams said. ‘‘But when it’s time to be in control, when it’s time to lock in and look the guys in the eyes, they want to feel your control over yourself, your control of the huddle. And then from there we can go out there and execute.’’</p><p>It was one of the best performances of Williams’ career. Given the stakes, it might have been the most important. The Bears were at a ‘‘crossroads,’’ coach Ben Johnson said, after losing to the Packers. Williams reset their direction. His teammates felt it.</p><p>‘‘He has the juice,’’ Odunze said.</p><p>As an added bonus, Williams said his hamstring wasn’t sore after the game, though he’ll need to continue treatment for it through the rest of the season. Williams ran four times for three yards, including a two-yard sneak for a first down with 2:46 lefty. That was far different than his last complete game, when he ran 10 times for 65 yards in Week 1.</p><p>This was the dream scenario the Bears had in mind when they decided to start Williams a week after Tyson Bagent struggled against the Packers. The plan started with a brief meeting in Johnson’s office early last week.</p><p>‘‘I walked in his office, dapped him up and said, ‘Let’s get this going this week,’ ’’ Williams said. ‘‘And I walked out after that.’’</p><p>The energy from Williams’ return crackled through the stadium. The Bears led 14-0 at the end of the first quarter and never trailed. There were so many Bears fans inside Mercedes-Benz Stadium that the Falcons practiced all week with crowd noise and used a silent count on offense. The crowd erupted with every Williams success.</p><p>The Bears’ defense felt the energy, too, giving up seven points through the first three quarters. The Falcons rallied for 16 points in the fourth and marched for a touchdown against Bears backups before Johnson put the starters back in. The Bears were trying to lighten the defensive workload with a game Thursday against the Patriots, Johnson said, but reversed course to lock down the victory.</p><p>The Bears’ special-teamers got in on the act, too, recovering a fumbled kickoff and a muffed punt — the latter on Tory Taylor’s curving ‘‘banana ball’’ — that contributed to 10 points.</p><p>‘‘The fact that we started fast, really in all three phases, was huge for us, as well as something that we had also talked about the night before,’’ Johnson said. ‘‘If you could write a script, that’s what we would want to do against a team like this. We’ve got to come out of the gate hot.’’</p><p>Earlier in the week, it was Williams who was hot. He used his first news conference since Sept. 23 to rail against what he said were erroneous reports about the severity of his injury. What went unspoken was his<br>annoyance with those who mocked him leaving the game against the Vikings emotional and on a golf cart.</p><p>Williams made no mention of that beef after the game. But as he jogged to the locker room after the victory, he looked at the assembled media and, with a smile, paraphrased an old Kirk Cousins line.</p><p>‘‘Y’all like that?’’ he said.</p><p>The answer from the teammates waiting for him in the locker room — and from fans at home and in the stadium — was a resounding yes.</p><p>When Williams entered the locker room, he got a game ball. He told his teammates how hard it was to fight through the injury.</p><p>‘‘It was just me having a consistent positive mindset throughout the weeks over myself — and about myself — of being able to get back, trying to get back, fighting to get back,’’ Williams said. ‘‘And when I get back, just to show them who I am. And who we are.’’</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/18/bears-falcons-grades-caleb-williams-kyler-gordon-colston-loveland-chicago-atlanta-nfl" >Bears’ grades are in. entries.title: City Colleges of Chicago reach late-night tentative contract agreement to avoid strike
entries.summary: <p>The Cook County College Teachers Union, Local 1600, and the City Colleges of Chicago reached an overnight tentative contract agreement just hours before a strike was set to kick off Monday. </p><p>The contract is for four years and includes salaries that keep pace with inflation, protected health insurance, safeguards toward AI and a path toward free developmental education, according to a press release from the union. </p><p>"I am proud of our negotiating teams, of our members who were prepared to strike, and of this contract,” said CCCTU President Tony Johnston. “It should not have taken until 3:45 a.m. the day of a strike to get here. But we are happy to reach a fair agreement that supports students, faculty, and professionals.”</p><p>The agreement must now go to the membership for a ratification vote. If members approve, the agreement will go to the City Colleges Board of Trustees for approval.</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Family holiday gatherings feel lonely for single guy
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I'm a single male who's happy with his life, with plenty of friends and family. My issue is what I endure during the holidays. Every year, I'm invited over to Thanksgiving and Christmas, and I look forward to seeing family that I only see once or twice a year.</p><p>These get-togethers usually consist of 15 to 25 people. Yet, other than having the chance to say hello and goodbye, everyone breaks into cliques while I sit there the whole time with no one ever showing any interest in engaging in conversation with me. I've reached the point where this isolation has me feeling depressed and lonely even though I'm surrounded by people.</p><p>I've come to realize I'd be happier spending the holidays by myself. Would it be wrong to start declining these invitations and politely explain why? I mentioned this to family members in the past, and they've acknowledged the issue, but it continues to happen every time. — <i>INVISIBLE IN THE CROWD</i></p><p><b>DEAR INVISIBLE:</b> You are in charge of your own destiny. You don't have to sit on the sofa watching the rest of the guests socialize with each other. You could get up, walk over to the various groups and attempt to join the conversation. You could also go to these gatherings for a short time to wish your relatives a Happy Thanksgiving, Merry Christmas, Happy New Year, etc., and then leave to do something with friends or return home. As to explaining your absence to your hosts, it's not necessary to state your reason for skipping the event.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My maid of honor and I aren't seeing eye to eye on my bridal shower. I was clear about not wanting a surprise shower and about my wish to be kept informed about the preparation. She had decided to plan a surprise shower with a guest list of only 20 people. When she found out I wanted one with about 40 people (I have a large family and a moderate number of close friends), she got upset. She said I shouldn't be involved at all in the planning and that it's not proper etiquette.</p><p>Knowing her financial situation, I offered to cover the expenses and participate in the planning process. However, she isn't willing to accept my help. She believes that this isn't the way it should be and said she won't be able to plan it the way I want. She has now decided to forgo any role in planning it. Who is in the wrong here? — <i>ALMOST-BRIDE IN THE EAST</i></p><p><b>DEAR ALMOST-BRIDE:</b> She is. Because she's unwilling to coordinate with you and isn't comfortable with you paying for the shower she's unable to afford, she has done you a favor by speaking up now. (She has also indicated that maybe she's not maid of honor material.) Since you want a much larger shower than she was willing to provide, perhaps another friend or relative of yours will be willing to step in and help you plan the shower you were hoping for.</p><p>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127. </p>

entries.title: A new Chicago brewery is creating Korea’s oldest alcoholic drink
entries.summary: <p>Korea’s oldest alcoholic drink is now being brewed in Chicago.</p><p>Yido on the Near West Side specializes in brewing makgeolli, an unfiltered rice wine that’s naturally fermented with a starter culture — similar to kombucha. The drink is often described as being creamy, tart and sweet with fruity notes.</p><p>“I feel like Chicago is a city that's like a food and drink city,” Yido Brews founder Peter Quinn Woo Chung said. “It really cares about local craft and artisan creators, and so it just seemed like a big unfilled gap.”</p><p>Makgeolli has slowly <a class="Link" href="https://www.saveur.com/food/hana-makgeolli-alice-jun-spreading-korean-alcohol-and-culture/" target="_blank" ><u>grown in popularity</u></a> <a class="Link" href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/annakang/2020/05/15/korean-makgeolli-the-next-alcohol-trend-to-watch/?sh=7d04309b6740" target="_blank" ><u>in the U.S.</u></a> In South Korea, there are over <a class="Link" href="https://www.saveur.com/food/hana-makgeolli-alice-jun-spreading-korean-alcohol-and-culture/" target="_blank" ><u>760 licensed breweries</u></a> that produce over 2,000 varieties of the drink. In 2020, Hana Makgeolli opened in New York City – and it was known as the <a class="Link" href="https://www.mashed.com/1176649/new-york-city-is-home-to-the-only-makgeolli-brewery-in-the-us/" target="_blank" ><u>only commercial makgeolli brewery in U.S</u></a>. at the time. Since then, a handful more have opened across the country, including in <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/sangmakgeolli/?hl=en" target="_blank" ><u>California</u></a>, <a class="Link" href="https://jsbrewery.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Maryland</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://rainbrew.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Washington</u></a>.</p><div class="Enhancement" entries.title: Almost all lawsuits brought in Chicago's federal court over deadly Boeing 737 MAX crashes have been resolved
entries.summary: <p>Sales of Boeing Co.’s 737 MAX jetliners are soaring, with orders of the aircraft reaching record levels this year.</p><p>Boeing is also nearing a darker milestone. It’s resolved almost all litigation brought by families of the nearly 350 people killed in two overseas 737 MAX crashes, with a jury awarding the survivors of one of those who perished, Michael “Mick” Ryan, $29 million in August in Chicago’s federal courthouse.</p><p>Earlier in the year, a Chicago jury awarded the survivors of Samya Stumo nearly $50 million.</p><p>And last fall, a Chicago jury awarded about $28 million to the family of another crash victim, Shikha Garg.</p><p>Because Boeing was based in Chicago until its headquarters moved to Arlington, Virginia, in recent years, hundreds of lawsuits were centered at the Dirksen Federal Building in the South Loop.</p><p>While there were several high-profile verdicts within the last year, the vast majority of the cases were settled before they could go to trial and with confidentiality clauses.</p><p>Accordingly, plaintiff lawyers and Boeing officials won’t say how much has been paid out so far in total, though it’s likely in the billions of dollars.</p><p>And that doesn’t include costs and penalties associated with other legal problems that followed the 737 MAX crashes, including a now-concluded U.S. Justice Department investigation.</p><p>One 737 MAX crashed in 2018 shortly after taking off from an Indonesian airport, killing all 189 people aboard. In 2019, another 737 MAX went down in Ethiopia, killing all 157 on board.</p><p>Boeing initially tried blaming the pilots. But a flawed system that can affect flight controls — a system Boeing wasn’t truthful about with federal regulators, the airlines or the public — turned out to be a factor in both crashes.</p><p>The model was temporarily grounded while problems were fixed.</p><p>Boeing’s image has taken a beating ever since, and other problems have emerged, including in 2024 when a door plug on a 737 MAX blew out after departing Portland, Oregon.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b10000" entries.title: Gov. JB Pritzker signals more optimism on Bears stadium deal — maybe even in Chicago — as election nears
entries.summary: <p>Landing a stadium deal for a professional sports team is a delicate proposition for any elected official.</p><p>Nobody wants to give the farm away to a multibillion-dollar franchise like the Chicago Bears, but the alternative is just as bad — especially in a football-crazed state like Illinois.</p><p>“I’m just glad I’m not going to be known as the governor that lost the Bears,” Republican gubernatorial nominee Darren Bailey said in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/10/13/watch-illinois-gov-debate-jb-pritzker-darren-bailey-takeaways" target="_blank" ><u>a debate last week</u></a> with Gov. JB Pritzker, seemingly resigned to the team’s Indiana defection.</p><p>But as the Nov. 3 election nears, Pritzker has indicated he’s increasingly confident he and other Democratic leaders in Springfield can get the best of both worlds while carrying a stadium deal across the goal line.</p><p>The incumbent’s optimism seems to be cresting for a resolution arriving five years after the Bears’ drive for a new home began, 11 months after the team’s first Hoosier threat — and a few weeks after the polls close.</p><p>And it could even happen in Chicago, Pritzker says, which had been all but eliminated from the Bears’ conversation for the past year in favor of Arlington Heights.</p><p>“I believe that in November, we’re going to be able to get something done to keep the Bears in the state of Illinois,” Pritzker said. “But I’m not going to do it at the expense of the taxpayers.”</p><p>Convenient timing, if you ask Bailey, who’s trying to win over voters himself in his second bid to unseat Pritzker. Lawmakers return to Springfield two weeks after the Nov. 3 election.</p><p>But the GOP challenger’s proposal to keep the Bears in their home state sounds remarkably similar to ones Pritzker has supported over his tenure. The same goes for independent gubernatorial candidate Collin Corbett, who agrees it should be a priority.</p><p>“If you're ever going to turn around the reputation of a state like Illinois, the Bears are one business, but they're a very public and a very loud business,” Corbett said. “We need to show that we're open for business, that we want to grow, and no, that doesn't mean you're going to get a big, sweetheart deal.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-810000" class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided by Manica Architecture</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Another tone shift in stadium talks</b></h3><p>Pritzker has rejected the prospect of any giveaways for the Bears since the McCaskeys entered a deal to acquire the old Arlington International Racecourse property in 2021.</p><p>But <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/01/16/chicago-bears-stadium-northwest-indiana-arlington-heights-jb-pritzker-kam-buckner" target="_blank" ><u>the governor’s tone changed considerably</u></a> after the team’s threat last fall to move to Indiana, following years of Chicago legislators rolling their eyes at overtures for a bill affording the Bears long-term property tax breaks on the 326-acre northwest suburban site.</p><p>Pritzker backed off previous suggestions the Bears should pay off lingering debt from Soldier Field’s 2003 renovation and began emphasizing his support for public funding of potentially hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of infrastructure upgrades around a potential dome.</p><p>Most importantly, Pritzker took on a more active role in stadium negotiations than the passive presence from his office that lobbyists and some legislators close to the discussions had privately grumbled about for years.</p><p>The governor is driving the talks now, meeting again earlier this month with NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell, whose repeated visits to Illinois might suggest the league’s not thrilled at the prospect of breaking ground on a Hammond dome.</p><p>Pritzker has supported the broader concept of allowing the Bears to negotiate a discounted payment in lieu of taxes (PILOT) with local governments. The Illinois House passed such a bill this spring, earning critical support from Chicago Democrats because it would’ve shared proceeds with homeowners as property tax rebates — but those returns were deemed “<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/04/bears-stadium-property-tax-relief-pritzker-negligible" target="_blank" ><u>negligible</u></a>.”</p><p>The Illinois Senate passed a separate bill that would allow municipalities to create their own stadium authorities to negotiate terms of a publicly owned stadium, but it crumbled in the waning hours of spring session <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/31/bears-stadium-bill-springfield-arlington-heights-hammond-indiana" target="_blank" ><u>without a vote in the other chamber</u></a>.</p><p>Sources familiar with the negotiations say the conversation has shifted toward the stadium authority model. That would mean no tax bill for the Bears — and it'd keep the door open to Chicago, providing vital cover for city legislators loath to pave the team's path to Arlington Heights.</p><p>While there hasn’t been a clear breakthrough, optimism is growing for a bill to move by January’s lame-duck session, if not this fall’s veto session. Pritzker raised the stakes by taking the under on that timeline.</p><p>“The legislation that is being discussed now would give the option for the possibility that there would be a stadium built in the city or in Arlington Heights,” Pritzker said last week. “We want to keep them in the state of Illinois. If we give them those two options, I think that would be satisfactory.</p><p>“In the end, this is up to the Bears,” he added.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-100000" name="image-100000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/618c9c1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6048x3394+0+319/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fdd%2F99%2Fa55ca32b4ba98cae3aecdbe43a21%2Fgovdebate-261015-14.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ff35a8a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6048x3394+0+319/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fdd%2F99%2Fa55ca32b4ba98cae3aecdbe43a21%2Fgovdebate-261015-14.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a307320/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6048x3394+0+319/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fdd%2F99%2Fa55ca32b4ba98cae3aecdbe43a21%2Fgovdebate-261015-14.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Republican nominee Darren Bailey laughs beside Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker before the start of the televised WTTW News Gubernatorial Forum on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Victor Hilitski/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>A familiar Bears stadium pitch from Darren Bailey</b></h3><p>Bailey, taking <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/10/13/jb-pritzker-darren-bailey-collin-corbett-illinois-governor-election-november-midterm" >another shot at the gubernatorial end zone</a> four years after losing to Pritzker, suggested a Bears move to Indiana is a fait accompli based on his own conversations with Indiana Gov. Mike Braun. Hoosier lawmakers rolled out the red carpet in February with a generous legislative package that would put $1 billion into a Bears dome.</p><p>But last month, Bailey wore a Bears jersey while offering up his own so-called “I-Formation Plan” to entice the team to stay in-state.</p><p>The crux of the downstate proposal is a PILOT incentive similar to what Pritzker has supported, which passed the Illinois House but was dead on arrival amid stiff opposition from Chicago Democrats in the state Senate.</p><p>“Rejecting a bad deal does not excuse JB Pritzker from finding a better one,” Bailey said. “That's what governors are elected to do. They're supposed to be bringing people together. They're supposed to negotiate. They're supposed to protect taxpayers, and they're supposed to deliver a solution. Instead, JB Pritzker has allowed years to pass while Indiana aggressively pursued our team.”</p><p>Bailey’s running mate, Aaron Del Mar, said Pritzker should have been able to whip the votes.</p><p>“JB Pritzker, who is the leader of the Democratic Party, is the largest funder of the Democratic Party of Illinois, needs to start putting some political pressure on his own people,” Del Mar said.</p><h3><b>Independent take</b></h3><p>Corbett, the former Republican strategist mounting a moderate independent campaign, agreed the onus was on Pritzker to get Chicago Democrats in line with a PILOT model.</p><p>“His entire economic development strategy is giving these big taxpayer benefits to big corporations, so I do believe it's him talking out of both sides of his mouth,” said Corbett, a Palatine resident.</p><p>“He knows that if he wants to run for president and win a Democratic primary, he can't be the guy who gave a billionaire sports franchise a tax break. And that's the problem here — politics is what has gotten in the way.”</p><p>That means twisting some legislative arms in the city, for the sake of not sending a $9 billion franchise across the border.</p><p>“If we're one Illinois, and what's good for Chicago is good for the rest of the state — well, then that has to go in both directions,” Corbett said.</p>
